entry.title: A Blueprint for National and International Healthcare Data Ecosystems: Learning From Building STRONG ‐ AYA
entry.summary:
Learning Health Systems · 2026-11-08 · group authors: Leonard Wee
Introduction: Healthcare systems aim for continuous improvement to ensure excellent clinical outcomes, including optimized quality of life. This relies on accurate data and evaluation patient-centered as well as biomedical outcomes. This data increasingly arises from real-world data (RWD). We are using this data across a multi-national European consortium, to create a Learning Healthcare System, improve care, policy, and ultimately patients' outcomes. Methods: STRONG-AYA is an interdisciplinary community, led from the Netherlands Cancer Institute, working across frequent consensus meetings, surveys, questionnaire design, data collection, synthesis and privacy-preserving federated analysis (in Vantage6), to ethically study and apply clinical and patient-centered outcomes data to learn about healthcare systems for Adolescents and Young Adults (AYAs) diagnosed with cancer when aged 15-39. The young people themselves are at the heart of our decision-making, and we work to make our data analyses transparent. Results: A harmonized 'Core Outcome Set' was agreed with all stakeholders. We developed definitions and data science methodological approaches, aligned with Learning Healthcare System practices. We have built AYA cancer data ecosystems, at local, national and European levels, to combine informatics with lived experience, clinical and scientific interpretation, based upon initial 'use cases' of the mental health consequences and cancer survival rates. We are applying those insights in real time individual clinical care, individual patient education and support as well as service level metrics. Conclusions: The Strong-AYA Learning Healthcare System for AYA-onset cancer can empower discovery by health researchers, digital innovation, and innovative insights for patients, clinicians, managers and policymakers who aim for transformational improvements in the quality and outcomes of current clinical practice though the development of a Learning Healthcare System in AYA-onset cancer care. Sustainability is our next major challenge.

entry.title: Stakeholder perspectives on implementing geographic information systems for leprosy elimination in Pakistan: A qualitative study
entry.summary:
PLoS ONE · 2026-11-05 · group authors: Johan van Soest
INTRODUCTION: Leprosy remains a pressing global health concern, with Pakistan among countries still facing missed and delayed diagnosis. By highlighting elevated risk areas, Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are a cost-effective solution to improve leprosy case detection by guiding targeted interventions to high-risk areas. This study's purpose was to investigate the perceived GIS implementation facilitators and barriers, to support targeted interventions and advance the Zero Leprosy strategy. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with twelve stakeholders, including local field staff, program managers, and international experts. Thematic analysis was guided by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and the Diffusion of Innovation Theory (DOI) to identify facilitators and barriers concerned with GIS implementation for leprosy. RESULTS: Key facilitators included an integrated multi-disease and pilot-based rollout approach, capacity building activities, offline-capable tools, and improved visibility to drive motivation. Barriers included the limited local capacity in complex GIS data analysis, hybrid digital-manual workflows, historical data lacking GPS, and ensuring feedback and ownership for staff members. CONCLUSION: GIS implementation is not only dependent on individual readiness, but also on broader external and organizational facilitators and constraints. This necessitates holistic implementation strategies that recognize the interconnectedness of different parts of the system. Internal capacity building is paramount to address statistical complexity and to build trust, ownership, and independence. As the world moves closer to achieving Zero Leprosy, integrating GIS within a multi-disease approach will be critical to making sustainable progress in combatting neglected tropical diseases.

entry.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Semi-automated Personal Health Data Curation and Reuse for Myocardial Infarction
entry.summary:
European Heart Journal - Digital Health · 2026-11-03 · group authors: Wenjie Liang, Rutger van Mierlo, Cecile Wolfs, Aiara Lobo Gomes, Andre Dekker, Petros Kalendralis
Abstract Background and Aims Digital applications have high potential in myocardial infarction management. This study aims to harmonize personal health data using a workflow driven by an Artificial Intelligence-assisted virtual assistant prototype, then reuse the data to facilitate the creation of standardized patient summaries and risk assessment. Methods The required configurations for data documentation and curation were developed to drive the workflow execution. With consent and data transfer agreements, data of patients with myocardial infarction were extracted from multi-source medical records, structured and ingested into the workflow. After transformation, personal health data were mapped into concrete clinical concepts connected with specific relationships defined by the reference ontology, forming source health knowledge graphs as the basic structure of personal health knowledge graphs. Then the constructed graphs were validated by using Shapes Constraint Language-based constraints, triggering the human-in-the-loop process to enhance data quality. Information queries were conducted for data reuse. Results 38 out of 45 planned patients were recruited with a signed informed consent. Thirty patients finalized the study. Overall successful data ingestion rate is approximately 83%. The average data quality score is 95.45/100. Constructed personal health knowledge graphs can be reused to represent medical information as an international patient summary and evaluate individual risk of future cardiovascular events by calculating the Second Manifestations of Arterial Disease risk score. Conclusion Our proposed workflow is feasible for semi-automated personal health data curation and secondary use. It provides a potential solution to enhance medical data interoperability, thereby facilitating risk assessment in cardiovascular diseases.

entry.title: AB025. Deep learning model predicts recurrence in thymic epithelial tumours: a multicentre study
entry.summary:
Mediastinum · 2026-10-01 · group authors: Rianne Fijten
BACKGROUND: Thymic epithelial tumours (TETs) are the most common primary neoplasms of the anterior mediastinum. Despite complete surgical resection (R0), a significant proportion of patients experience recurrence, highlighting the need for improved prognostic stratification. Morphological patterns recognised in clinical practice may have prognostic value, and this study applies deep learning (DL) to haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole slide images (WSIs) to predict recurrence in TETs, assisting pathologists in risk assessment and enabling precise treatment planning. METHODS: A multicentre cohort of resected TET patients with complete (R0) resection and no distant metastasis was assembled from Erasmus Medical Centre (EMC), Maastricht University Medical Centre (MUMC+) and the TCGA public dataset, with an external validation cohort from Hospices Civils de Lyon (HCL). WSIs were annotated in QuPath and sampled at 20× magnification into 512×512 patches. HCL WSIs, stained with haematoxylin-eosin saffron, underwent Vahadane normalisation to harmonise staining across centres. Patch embeddings from a pretrained Phikon encoder were aggregated through a multi-instance learning for patient level recurrence prediction, using stratified three-fold cross-validation. GradCAM applied to the most contributing patches generated heatmaps of the areas of highest model activation. RESULTS: Recurrence occurred in 19 of 298 patients (6.4%) internally and 5 of 95 (5.3%) externally. The model achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.85, a balanced accuracy (BAcc) of 0.71, and sensitivity of 79% internally. Performance was preserved externally (AUC 0.70, BAcc 0.62, sensitivity 80%) despite domain shift. In true positive cases, heatmaps consistently localised to tumour tissue adjacent to fibrous septa, capsular structures and vascular interfaces, with additional focal activation in areas of increased cellular heterogeneity in tumours lacking prominent separation. CONCLUSIONS: The DL model can identify TET patients at risk of recurrence following R0 resection and demonstrates generalisability across institutions with differing tissue preparation protocols. Heatmaps corresponded to septal, capsular and perivascular structures, sites classically associated with tumour invasion and recurrence risk in TETs, suggesting the model may capture histological correlates of invasive behaviour. Future work will focus on larger datasets, multimodal architectures integrating clinical and imaging data, and further external validation.

entry.title: AB024. Mixed histology is a prognostic factor for recurrence in completely resected thymic epithelial tumours: a multicentre retrospective study
entry.summary:
Mediastinum · 2026-10-01 · group authors: Rianne Fijten
BACKGROUND: The recurrence of thymic epithelial tumours (TETs) following complete resection remains unpredictable. While the Masaoka-Koga staging system and WHO subtype classification are useful for clinical decision-making, no externally validated prognostic model exists to inform risk-adapted follow-up. Tumours with composite histological patterns, such as B2+B3 or B3+TC, are usually classified by their dominant subtype, potentially underestimating their aggressiveness. This study aimed to determine whether a machine learning (ML) model using these routine pathological variables could predict recurrence in completely resected TETs and whether including mixed histology would improve risk stratification. METHODS: Clinical data were collected from four centres (EMC, UMC+, TCGA and HCL). Patients with R1/R2 resection or stage IV disease were excluded. An internal development cohort (EMC (n=89), UMC+ (n=102), TCGA (n=116) and a geographically independent external validation cohort (HCL, n=95) were defined. A binary variable was introduced to identify tumours presenting two or more WHO subtypes. Six ML algorithms were evaluated and explainability was ensured through SHAP-based feature attribution. RESULTS: Patients with mixed histology had a recurrence rate of 18.5% (5/27) compared to 5.1% (14/277) in single-subtype cases (χ²=5.49, P=0.02). Among the six algorithms, Random Forest achieved the most consistent performance, with a balanced accuracy (BAcc) of 0.73 and Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.73 on the internal development cohort and a BAcc of 0.73, AUC of 0.72 and sensitivity of 0.80 on the external validation cohort. Ablation analysis confirmed the independent contribution of the mixed subtype indicator, as its removal reduced specificity by 0.03 and 0.08 in the internal and external cohorts respectively. SHAP analysis revealed that Masaoka-Koga stage IIb and subtype B2 had the highest feature importance, partly reflecting their prevalence in the dataset. Importantly, the overall pattern was consistent with established clinical knowledge, that aggressive subtypes and higher stages driving recurrence and indolent subtypes acting as protective, suggesting the model learned authentic clinicopathological relationships. CONCLUSIONS: We developed an interpretable, externally validated model built on routine pathology data achieved clinically meaningful recurrence prediction in completely resected TETs. Our results support formal recognition of mixed histological subtypes as an independent risk factor and their inclusion in pathology may improve postoperative risk stratification.

entry.title: Brain state locks silent memories in a trained fly connectome
entry.summary:
bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory) · 2026-10-29 · group authors: Xuanhe Hou
SUMMARY Complete connectomes now exist for insect nervous systems, but whether a fixed wiring diagram can learn, and what its memories consist of, is unknown. Here, we trained a spiking model of the whole male Drosophila central nervous system, 167,106 neurons with fixed wiring, to plan moves and to remember a visual cue. Spikes write the cue into neuronal adaptation, which holds it silently until the next input reads it out. Cells that hold the trace are enriched for transcripts of a calcium-activated potassium channel in fly cell atlases. The learned readout recalls the trace only in the brain state of learning: the same trace evokes a different response at another delay, and a disease-like loss of potassium current rewrites the trace and changes how it is read. Learning in the new state is spared. Memory failure can arise from a change of state rather than a loss of storage. HIGHLIGHTS A fixed whole-fly connectome learns to plan and to remember a visual cue The cue is held silently in neuronal adaptation and read out by the next input Recall works only in the brain state of learning, at writing and at reading A disease-like lesion rewrites the trace, while learning in the new state is spared IN BRIEF Wang et al. train a spiking model of the whole male fly nervous system to plan and to remember. It holds a visual cue silently in neuronal adaptation and recalls it only in the brain state of learning, so a disease-like lesion removes recall while new learning is spared.

entry.title: The limits of privacy enhancement in healthcare federated learning: a ELSA perspective in the EU context
entry.summary:
Frontiers in Big Data · 2026-10-29 · group authors: Marine Jacquemin
Federated Learning (FL) usage is steadily increasing in healthcare. Offering an attractive alternative to centralized data processing, FL is often promoted as a privacy-enhancing technology (PET) because it keeps patient-level data local, exchanging only aggregated data or model updates. As such, it is frequently presented as a means of addressing the ethical, legal and societal challenges associated with the use of sensitive health data. This framing has contributed to growing policy interest in FL within initiatives such as the European Health Data Space (EHDS). This paper examines FL from an ethical, legal and societal (ELSA) perspective in the EU context, focusing on its interaction with the European data protection framework and contemporary debates on health data governance. First, it analyzes the interaction between FL architectures and the General Data Protection regulation (GDPR), showing that questions of controllership, joint responsibility, and identifiability persist despite decentralization, particularly in complex multi-institutional settings. Second, it argues that privacy-centric approaches to health data governance remain ethically insufficient because harmful inferences, discrimination, and collective harms may arise even when data remains formally anonymous. The dominant focus on reidentification risk thus reflects a narrow and individualistic conception of privacy that is poorly adapted to the contemporary data landscape of the EU. It fails to capture broader forms of harm, including group-level discrimination, inferential profiling, and structural power asymmetries. The paper concludes that, despite its framing as a PET, the use of FL alone is not sufficient to guarantee appropriate health data protection. Indeed, FL should also be approached as a distributed data-processing paradigm in which risks and benefits depend on implementation choices, institutional arrangements, and regulatory interpretation. Accordingly, FL should be situated within broader questions of data governance, including how access, accountability, and collaboration are structured and distributed across institutions.

entry.title: Generating patient-friendly radiology reports with a local large language model: expert evaluation of quality and readability
entry.summary:
European Radiology · 2026-10-29 · group authors: Sander Puts, Martijn Nobel
OBJECTIVES: To assess the feasibility of using a locally hosted large language model (LLM) to generate patient-friendly radiology reports while avoiding cloud transfer of report text. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective study, 360 chest, knee, lumbar spine, and shoulder X-rays, and shoulder and abdominal ultrasound reports from Dutch primary care were included. Main report sections (n = 359) and conclusion sections (n = 350) were translated into patient-friendly versions using Gemma-3 (12B parameters) and assessed for accuracy and completeness on 5-point Likert scales. Readability was evaluated using text length and Flesch-Douma reading ease (FDRE) scores. Hallucinations were systematically documented. Statistical analyses included Kruskal-Wallis, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and paired t-tests. RESULTS: Patient-friendly conclusions achieved higher median accuracy scores than main reports (5 [Q1-Q3 5-5] vs 4 [3-5]), while completeness scores were high for both sections (5 [5-5]). Compared with original reports, patient-friendly reports were longer (median increase 65 words [48-84], p < 0.001) and had higher FDRE scores (mean increase 54.2 ± 18.8, p < 0.001). Overall, 71.0% of main reports and 96.0% of conclusions met predefined quality criteria (accuracy and completeness ≥ 4), while 48.0% of combined main report and conclusion sections met both quality and readability criteria (FDRE score > 60). Clinically relevant hallucinations occurred in 45 reports (12.5%). CONCLUSION: A locally hosted LLM demonstrated feasibility for generating patient-friendly translations of Dutch X-ray and ultrasound reports while avoiding cloud transfer of data, with better performance for conclusion sections than main reports. However, clinically relevant hallucinations remain a safety concern and indicate the need for clinician oversight and further evaluation before clinical implementation. KEY POINTS: Question Can a locally hosted LLM generate patient-friendly radiology reports while preserving data privacy and maintaining acceptable accuracy, completeness, and readability? Findings A locally hosted LLM generated patient-friendly report conclusions with higher quality scores than main reports, while clinically relevant hallucinations remained an important safety concern. Clinical relevance A locally hosted LLM has potential to generate patient-friendly radiology report translations without external cloud data transfer. Report conclusions appear to be the most promising initial application, although clinician oversight and further patient-centered validation remain essential before clinical implementation.

entry.title: IEKB: a comprehensive knowledge base for inner ear genetics integrating curated associations, cochlear interactions, Bayesian candidate prioritisation, explainable dark-gene support relations, and a scientific entity network
entry.summary:
bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory) · 2026-04-09 · group authors: Xuanhe Hou
Abstract Inner-ear genetics has expanded rapidly, yet the supporting evidence remains dispersed across a vast literature and across resources that typically emphasise loci, variants, or expression data rather than integrated biological interpretation. Here we present the Inner Ear Knowledge Base (IEKB; https://earkb.org ), an open database that unifies curated associations, cochlear interaction evidence, candidate prioritisation, explainable support relations, and network exploration for inner-ear research. IEKB was built with an automated agent-assisted curation workflow that combines schema-constrained literature extraction, continuous human monitoring, and final expert review by inner-ear genetics researchers. By systematically analysing 250,696 PubMed-indexed records retrieved across 16,563 screened genes, IEKB curates 6,051 gene–phenotype–disease associations from 2,494 genes across 43 phenotype categories and 4,102 cochlear gene–gene interactions with pathway, cell-type, and experimental context. IEKB further includes a Bayesian “dark matter” module that prioritises 243,071 candidate gene–phenotype associations for 13,229 genes across all 43 phenotypes (global AUC-ROC = 0.8603; global AUC-PR = 0.1674), together with a supervised dark-relation layer that ranks phenotype-specific known-gene support for each candidate and a multi-entity scientific network containing nearly 4,000 entities, 28,616 deterministic edges, and 83,712 literature-derived relational links. The web resource supports interactive search, multi-parameter filtering, gene-detail pages, bibliometric exploration, domain-specific enrichment against IEKB phenotype and disease gene sets, network visualisation, bulk download in CSV, JSON, SQLite, and XLSX formats, and natural-language evidence-grounded question answering through a companion conversational interface (IEKB QA). To our knowledge, IEKB is the first openly accessible inner-ear resource that integrates curated associations, cochlear interactions, probabilistic candidate prioritisation, auditable known-gene support relations for novel candidates, and a multi-entity scientific network within a single database. All data are released without registration under the CC BY 4.0 license.

entry.title: The impact of digital tools and the expected digital transformation in radiotherapy on Dutch radiation therapists (RTTs)
entry.summary:
Technical Innovations & Patient Support in Radiation Oncology · 2025-06-01 · group authors: Thijs Ackermans
Background and Purpose: Technological advancements have the potential to mitigate RTT shortages, burnout levels, and turnover rates. However, it is unclear if RTTs currently experience technostress (stress or anxiety from being overwhelmed by technology) and how extensive digital tool usage impacts key job performance indicators (e.g., job engagement, satisfaction, and turnover intentions). This study investigates the impact of digital tools used and expected digital transformation on RTTs' technostress and key job performance indicators. Materials and Methods: A survey was distributed to RTTs across all Dutch radiotherapy centers, resulting in 265 respondents. The survey included validated questionnaires on digital tool use, technostress, job autonomy, innovative work behavior and job performance indicators. Relationships were assessed using linear regression models and paired samples T-tests (p < 0.05). Results: The number of digital tools used had no significant effect (p < 0.05) on key job performance indicators and was not related to technostress. Technostress negatively impacted key job performance indicators, but explained less than 7 % of the variance. Other factors, such as job autonomy, had a greater influence. When presented with a description of the future perspective of their job role after the expected digital transformation, RTTs reported small declines in key job performance indicators. Conclusion: Current RTT performance is not affected by the number of digital tools used, as RTTs are used to working with digital tools. RTTs showed no technostress. After the predicted digital transformation RTTs remained satisfied and engaged. Ensuring RTTs feel skilled and empowered with decision-making authority is crucial before introducing new digital tools.

entry.title: Cross-disease multi-omics integration reveals shared mechanisms driving the breast cancer-rheumatoid arthritis association
entry.summary:
Next research. · 2026-08-07 · group authors: En Hu
Humans, as highly social organisms, maintain health through both physiological homeostasis and interactions within social environments. The immune system is central to this balance, and its dysregulation manifests in diverse pathologies. Breast cancer (BC), the most common malignancy among women, represents disrupted biological order through uncontrolled proliferation and immune escape, whereas rheumatoid arthritis (RA) reflects pathological immune hyperactivation and autoimmunity. Persistent inflammation and functional impairment in RA may influence breast cancer risk and prognosis, while breast cancer onset or treatment may exacerbate immune vulnerability. To elucidate mechanisms underlying these interconnected disease processes, we integrated large-scale genetic association analyses with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to dissect cross-disease convergence across organ systems, cellular regulation, and molecular networks. Our multimodal framework identified shared risk loci and mapped their regulatory consequences across tissues and cell states, providing mechanistic insights into developmental and immune pathways that may underlie the intrinsic connection between breast cancer and RA.

entry.title: D5.12 Causability Report and Impact on Explainability
entry.summary:
Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research) · 2026-07-06 · group authors: Rutger van Mierlo
This deliverable reports on the explainability/causability-related work done in Task 5.3 of the AIDAVA project. It briefly describes the conceptualisation of the explainability module which served as a blueprint for the explainability features implemented in the AIDAVA G2 prototype. The core emphasis of this deliverable is the formative causability evaluation of the implemented explainability features. The causability evaluation aimed to determine whether explanations were understandable, useful for users’ tasks, and free of missing or misleading information that could impair safe use. To achieve this, controlled user tests (n=6) were carried out in the causability lab using a think‑aloud protocol comprising five task‑based sessions, which covered the main explainability features of AIDAVA G2. Complementing these lab tests, explainability-related feedback was systematically collected via targeted questionnaires from curators/study nurses (n=9) participating in the AIDAVA G2 prototype assessment study in the Netherlands, Estonia, and Austria.Key findingsCausability evaluation results confirmed that the overall concept of the AIDAVA explainability module with layered information design and on-demand progressive disclosure is appropriate —users prefer concise top‑level explanations in lay language with optional deeper detail and tailoring to digital literacy.Identified strengths of the implemented explainability features included explicit “relevant part” text in human-in-the-loop (HITL) dialogues and visual highlighting of related source text which were deemed to be useful and valued when these worked as intended.Major weaknesses were confusing or misleading provenance views for International Patient Summary (IPS) entries, unclear attribution of human contributors in HITL interactions, overly technical and poorly structured descriptions of curation tools/processes, and critical safety messages buried in long global explanations.Perceived importance of explainability features varies by role and task: for test users in the lab tests (who assessed AIDAVA from point of view of patients) the most important explainability feature was the provenance of IPS entries since they wanted to understand curated results, while curators prioritized explanations that pinpoint which input triggered a HITL request and what issue the request aims to resolve since these explanations support their curation work.Recommendations for future developments to improve causability-Improve provenance: make “source” links open the source document and auto-highlight exact excerpt(s); show clear name, role and timestamp where humans entered data.-Simplify and structure explanations: default to brief, lay-language descriptions with clear “more information” links; make technical terms clickable for obtaining concise descriptions of their meaning, and provide expert-level links separately.-Make critical safety and AI-disclosure messages prominent on the pre-login and IPS screens.ConclusionThe AIDAVA G2 explainability module concept establishes a solid, principled foundation—modular, layered, and on-demand explanations—validated by formative testing. The causability evaluation identified clear, actionable improvements (provenance clarity, simplification of technical explanations, and consistent application of the principle of ‘progressive disclosure’ in all explanations) that are essential (future) steps towards a safe, trustworthy application and regulatory alignment.

entry.title: Monitoring cardiac symptoms during teleprehabilitation prior to coronary artery bypass grafting: a digital cardiac counselling trial subanalysis
entry.summary:
European Heart Journal - Digital Health · 2026-05-18 · group authors: Rutger van Mierlo
Abstract Aims The purpose of this subanalysis was to explore whether or not teleprehabilitation leads to worsening cardiac symptoms in patients accepted for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Methods and results A subgroup of patients accepted for CABG (including off-pump and minimally invasive) who were randomized between teleprehabilitation and standard care in DCC trial were included. Teleprehabilitation patients had access to blended care supported by online modules, including nutritional support, functional exercise training, smoking cessation, inspiratory muscle training, and psychological support. All patients were weekly telemonitored for cardiac symptoms using a customized digital platform. This cohort included 155 patients. Baseline characteristics, including NYHA and CCS class, were balanced, except for shorter preoperative waiting times in weeks (15.0 [9.8–22.2] vs. 12.5 [7.0–16.0]) in the teleprehabilitation group. There was no significant difference in incidence of major adverse cardiac events in the preoperative period. There were 141 patients (77 control; 64 teleprehabilitation) with at least one symptom monitoring entry. A total of 373/1786 (21%) entries indicated worsening of cardiac symptoms. The distribution was right-skewed and did not significantly differ between the two groups. There was no statistically significant difference in time to event between control and teleprehabilitation for any cardiac symptom (P = 0.529), angina (P = 0.167), or dyspnoea (P = 0.334). Conclusion Teleprehabilitation does not lead to worsening cardiac symptoms before CABG. We postulate that teleprehabilitation, which includes low-intensity physical training, can be safely offered to patients undergoing elective CABG.

entry.title: Transforming Histology into Virtual Multiplex Immunofluorescence to Decode Prognostic Spatial Immunity in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
entry.summary:
bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory) · 2026-02-26 · group authors: Wenjie Liang
Summary The spatial organization of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) drives hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) prognosis but remains unquantifiable on routine H&E slides. Here, we present HCCExplorer, a deep learning framework that translates H&E into virtual multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) and uses multi-modal graph learning to decode spatial survival signals. Trained on 30 H&E-mIF slide pairs, HCCExplorer evaluated a 1,813-slide multi-center cohort. It achieved superior overall survival stratification over clinical indices and state-of-the-art pathology and protein foundation models, yielding a concordance index of 0.71 and a Hazard Ratio (HR) of 15.46 ( P < 0.001), maintaining stability across three external cohorts. Beyond risk stratification, interpretation of model features identified M1 macrophage infiltration as a protective determinant (HR=0.40, P < 0.05). Furthermore, it uncovered a protective “Containment Niche” at the invasion frontier (HR=0.02, P < 0.01), featuring macrophages co-localizing with Foxp3+ Tregs and CD4+ T cells. Ultimately, HCCExplorer provides actionable, spatially-resolved biomarkers from conventional histology for precision HCC management.

entry.title: Super-resolution and habitat radiomics based computed tomography machine-learning model for prediction of lung invasive adenocarcinoma: a multi-centre study
entry.summary:
Quantitative Imaging in Medicine and Surgery · 2026-02-13 · group authors: Wenjie Liang
Background: Early differentiation between invasive adenocarcinoma (IAC) and non-IAC pulmonary nodules is crucial for guiding clinical decision-making. Therefore, this study aimed to distinguish IAC from non-IAC pulmonary nodules using intra-tumor radiomics signatures, habitat radiomics analysis, and a combined nomogram by integrating generative adversarial network (GAN) based super-resolution reconstruction. Methods: 89 IAC cases; mean ± SD: 57.037±11.683 years) were included. Univariate and multivariate analyses were conducted to explore clinical characteristics. Radiomics features were extracted from intra-tumor regions and sub-regions. After feature selection, machine learning models, namely the Intra-Model and Habitat-Model, were developed. A combined nomogram integrating significant clinical factors, intra-tumor radiomics and habitat radiomics was constructed and evaluated using area under receiver operator characteristics curve (AUC), decision curve analysis (DCA), and other quantified metrics. Results: 0.875) in predicting IAC invasiveness. The combined nomogram demonstrated an incremental advancement in IAC stratification [training AUC: 0.907 (95% CI: 0.887-0.927); testing AUC: 0.895 (95% CI: 0.849-0.941)], with DCA confirming 28-34% net benefit improvement over single-modality approaches at critical thresholds (10-25% risk). Age (P<0.001) and nodule diameter (P<0.001), along with intra-tumor and habitat radiomics, were identified as key contributing factors. Conclusions: The spatially resolved habitat radiomics model exhibited higher discriminative accuracy than the classical intra-tumor radiomics model. The combined nomogram framework, which integrated intra-tumor radiomics, habitat radiomics, and significant clinical biomarkers, achieved state-of-the-art performance in IAC stratification. This framework provides a robust tool for precision therapeutic decision-making in pulmonary nodule management.

entry.title: A feasibility study of automating radiotherapy planning with large language model agents
entry.summary:
Physics in Medicine and Biology · 2025-03-12 · group authors: Minghua Li, Zhen Zhang
Abstract Objective. Radiotherapy planning requires significant expertise to balance tumor control and organ-at-risk (OAR) sparing. Automated planning can improve both efficiency and quality. This study introduces GPT-Plan, a novel multi-agent system powered by the GPT-4 family of large language models (LLMs), for automating the iterative radiotherapy plan optimization. Approach. GPT-Plan uses LLM-driven agents, mimicking the collaborative clinical workflow of a dosimetrist and physicist, to iteratively generate and evaluate text-based radiotherapy plans based on predefined criteria. Supporting tools assist the agents by leveraging historical plans, mitigating LLM hallucinations, and balancing exploration and exploitation. Performance was evaluated on 12 lung (IMRT) and 5 cervical (VMAT) cancer cases, benchmarked against the ECHO auto-planning method and manual plans. The impact of historical plan retrieval on efficiency was also assessed. Results. For IMRT lung cancer cases, GPT-Plan generated high-quality plans, demonstrating superior target coverage and homogeneity compared to ECHO while maintaining comparable or better OAR sparing. For VMAT cervical cancer cases, plan quality was comparable to a senior physicist and consistently superior to a junior physicist, particularly for OAR sparing. Retrieving historical plans significantly reduced the number of required optimization iterations for lung cases (p < 0.01) and yielded iteration counts comparable to those of the senior physicist for cervical cases (p = 0.313). Occasional LLM hallucinations have been mitigated by self-reflection mechanisms. One limitation was the inaccuracy of vision-based LLMs in interpreting dose images. Significance. This pioneering study demonstrates the feasibility of automating radiotherapy planning using LLM-powered agents for complex treatment decision-making tasks. While challenges remain in addressing LLM limitations, ongoing advancements hold potential for further refining and expanding GPT-Plan’s capabilities.
